[[File:Newton polytope of the short Weierstrass equation.svg|thumb|300x300px|class=skin-invert-image|The Newton polytope of the [[Cubic plane curve#Weierstrass normal form|short Weierstrass equation]] <math>y^2 = x^3 + ax + b</math>. The green points correspond to the powers of the polynomials in the equations. Since there is one integer interior lattice point, then the [[Genus (mathematics)|genus]] of the equation also equals to one.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sutherland |first=Andrew |date=2022-01-31 |title=18.783 Elliptic Curves Lecture 1 |url=https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2022/LectureSlides1.pdf#page=15}}</ref>]]
In mathematics, the '''Newton polytope''' is an [[integral polytope]] associated with a multivariate [[polynomial]] that can be used in the [[asymptotic analysis]] of those polynomials.  It is a generalization of the Kruskal{{endash}}Newton diagram developed for the analysis of bivariant polynomials.

Given a vector <math>\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> of variables and a finite family <math>(\mathbf{a}_k)_k</math> of pairwise distinct vectors from <math>\mathbb{N}^n</math> each encoding the exponents within a monomial, consider the multivariate polynomial

<math display=block>f(\mathbf{x})=\sum_k c_k\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{a}_k}</math>

where we use the shorthand notation <math>(x_1,\ldots,x_n)^{(y_1,\ldots,y_n)}</math> for the monomial <math>x_1^{y_1}x_2^{y_2}\cdots x_n^{y_n}</math>.  Then the Newton polytope associated to <math>f</math> is the [[convex hull]] of the vectors <math>\mathbf{a}_k</math>; that is

<math display=block>\operatorname{Newt}(f)=\left\{\sum_k \alpha_k\mathbf{a}_k :\sum_k \alpha_k =1\;\&\;\forall j\,\,\alpha_j\geq0\right\}\!.</math>

In order to make this well-defined, we assume that all coefficients <math>c_k</math> are non-zero. The Newton polytope satisfies the following homomorphism-type property: 
<math display=block>\operatorname{Newt}(fg)=\operatorname{Newt}(f)+\operatorname{Newt}(g)</math>
where the addition is in [[Minkowski sum|the sense of Minkowski]].

Newton polytopes are the central object of study in [[tropical geometry]] and characterize the [[Gröbner basis|Gröbner bases for an ideal]].
